tier_reason: The README's 500M-call table (luajit 891/905 ms, c 1182/1182, cpp 1182/1183) comes from public code (hello.c, hello.cpp, hello.lua, newplus/plus.c, Tupfile, Tuprules.tup with -O2 -fPIC), with gcc 5.4.1, luajit 2.0.4 and an i7-3630QM stated, so on paper the methodology reaches A. It is held at C because the C side is -O2 (wave 14 asks for -O3) and the win comes from call linkage, not the language: the C executable calls plusone through the PLT of libnewplus.so while LuaJIT calls the dlsym-resolved address, and an independent C benchmark (skeeto/dynamic-function-benchmark, -O3, i7-6700) shows C itself reaching direct-call speed (1.01 ns vs 1.76 ns through the PLT). This follows the sort-self precedent: A methodology, but the mechanism is not the language.

corrections.claimed_speedup: LuaJIT 891 ms and 905 ms vs C 1182 and 1182 ms (C++ 1182 and 1183 ms) for 500M calls of plusone() in libnewplus.so: about 1.3x faster, 1.78 vs 2.36 ns per call (derived from page data). Julia 0.6.3 ccall (894 and 889 ms) wins by the same margin.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C and C++: gcc/g++ 5.4.1 with -O2 -fPIC -Wall -Wextra (Tuprules.tup CFLAGS; C++ adds -std=c++14 -fno-rtti). The executables are linked at -O2 with -Lnewplus -lnewplus -Wl,-rpath,$ORIGIN/newplus (Tupfile), so each call to plusone goes through the PLT; gcc 5.4 has no -fno-plt. libnewplus.so is built from newplus/plus.c with the same -O2 -fPIC. LuaJIT 2.0.4 runs hello.lua with default JIT settings, loads the same .so with ffi.load and calls newplus.plusone. Julia 0.6.3 uses ccall. Ubuntu 14.04; 2 samples per language (run-all.sh); timing by gettimeofday in milliseconds (newplus/plus.c current_timestamp).
corrections.why_faster: From the sources: hello.c and hello.cpp call plusone() as an ordinary external function of libnewplus.so (linked with -lnewplus in the Tupfile), so every call goes through the PLT stub plus an indirect jump through the GOT. hello.lua binds the symbol with ffi.load (dlopen and dlsym), and LuaJIT's compiled trace calls the resolved address without a PLT stub. plusone cannot be inlined on either side. The gap of about 0.58 ns per call (derived) is in line with an independent C measurement of PLT versus direct calls (skeeto/dynamic-function-benchmark README: 1.76 vs 1.01 ns per call on an i7-6700 at -O3; 1.26 ns through a dlsym function pointer). So C calling through a dlsym'd pointer, a static link or -fno-plt would recover most or all of the gap. This is a linkage effect, not codegen or a language property.
corrections.caveats: Measures foreign-call overhead for a trivial function, not code quality. The C and C++ rows call through the PLT of a shared library; the LuaJIT FFI and Julia ccall paths call the resolved address directly. The independent skeeto/dynamic-function-benchmark (Unlicense; benchmark.c and Makefile with -O3 -fpie) shows plain C reaching the same direct-call speed (1.01 ns vs 1.76 ns through the PLT). The accompanying nullprogram.com article 'When FFI Function Calls Beat Native C' (2018-05-27) explains this exact ffi-overhead result by the PLT, but the blog was unreachable (search snippet only). Repo issue #15, open since 2019-12-16, asks for a direct-addressed (non-PLT) C/C++ row; it was never added. C is compiled at -O2, not -O3 (irrelevant to the call itself, since plusone sits in a separate shared object). The toolchains are from 2018 (luajit 2.0.4, julia 0.6.3, gcc 5.4.1 on Ubuntu 14.04). Only 2 samples per language are shown, timed with a millisecond gettimeofday clock. The loop is 'while (x < count) x = plusone(x)'; issue #13 notes that loop overhead is part of every row. Many other languages in the table are slower than C (Go 37,975 ms, Node 9,163 ms, Java 4,469 ms).

notes: Confirm at C. The numbers, flags and metadata check out (Apache-2.0, 698 stars, 45 forks, last commit 2023-07-12, abandoned). Shortcomings to record: the win is the PLT trampoline of a dynamically linked C call, not language codegen, as an independent C benchmark (skeeto/dynamic-function-benchmark) shows; C at -O2 rather than -O3; issue #15 (direct-call C row) has been open since 2019; 2018 toolchains, 2 samples, millisecond timer. D is arguable under the AssemblyScript build-default precedent. It is held at C because PLT linkage is how C normally calls a shared library and the effect is real and reproduced independently.

tier_reason: First-party README table from the port's own public harness (benchmark/bench_migrad_suite.jl, benchmark/cpp/cpp_bench.cxx, benchmark/compare_cpp.jl), with the CPU (Apple M3) and Julia 1.12 stated and the C++ upstream pinned in docs/UPSTREAM.md (GooFit/Minuit2 6.24.0, commit 57dc936). The C++ compiler is not named, and the flags are only implied by CMake's Release default, so it is not A; there is no independent run.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.12 (default -O2) with OpenBLAS 0.3.29 and BLAS threads set to 1 (benchmark/perf-config.toml); Julia times are BenchmarkTools medians of 50 samples (evals policy auto). C++: benchmark/cpp/CMakeLists.txt sets C++17 and CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release by default (CMake's Release flags for Clang and GCC are -O3 -DNDEBUG). It builds C++ Minuit2 from reference/Minuit2_cpp, a gitignored checkout that docs/UPSTREAM.md pins to GooFit/Minuit2 commit 57dc936a2b74d0b4dda1254c3dd63e7c61a97c84 (tag 6.24.0). C++ times are medians of 50 single-shot std::chrono samples. The C++ compiler is not named. Minuit2's CMakeLists has no BLAS dependency (it has its own small linear algebra), so 'single-threaded BLAS on both sides' only affects the Julia side.
corrections.workload: Wall time of one full MIGRAD minimization with Strategy(0) and no parameter limits, including construction of the cost function and its random data, on five objectives: quad_4d (4 parameters from 1.0, step 0.1), rosenbrock_2d (start -1.2, 1.0), rosenbrock_10d, gauss_ll_10_1000 (10 independent Gaussian means, 100 points each) and gauss_ll_2_100 (mu and sigma of a Gaussian NLL over 100 points). Medians of 50 samples per side.
corrections.why_faster: From the sources: C++ Minuit2 6.24.0 calls the user FCN through the virtual FCNBase::operator()(const std::vector<double>&), and MnUserFcn::operator() heap-allocates a fresh std::vector<double> of external parameters on every FCN call (its own source comment puts the cost at about 10% on Rosenbrock). NativeMinuit's CostFunction{F,T} is parametric on the function type, so the FCN call is statically dispatched and inlinable; CHANGELOG 0.3.1 says a JET test guards the MIGRAD hot path against runtime dispatch, and the scratch buffers are local to each migrad call. The gain is therefore library overhead (allocation and dispatch around a nanosecond-scale FCN). It shrinks to about 1.13x on gauss_ll_2_100, where the FCN does real work. It is not a codegen win, and a C++ minimizer with a templated FCN could do the same.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from the port's author, on microsecond toy objectives of 2 to 10 parameters where per-call overhead dominates. The table appears to date from the 0.1.0-alpha Phase 0 gate: the CHANGELOG entry of 2026-05-25 reports 'max ratio 0.887x, mean 0.47x', which matches the README rows, and the repo shows no rerun for the current 0.7.x code. The C++ side is Minuit2 6.24.0 (2021), pinned in docs/UPSTREAM.md, built from a gitignored checkout; newer ROOT Minuit2 releases were not compared. The C++ compiler is not named, though CMake's Release default is -O3 -DNDEBUG. The timed regions differ in setup: C++ builds MnUserParameters with std::string names per run, and Julia builds a CostFunction. The gauss_ll rows use different random datasets (Julia's global-RNG randn, which advances with every sample, vs a C++ mt19937_64 reseeded per run). The CHANGELOG says Rosenbrock results agree only 'within Strategy(0) cross-impl variance', and the README does not show the nfcn per fit, so equal work per fit is not demonstrated. CHANGELOG 0.7.1 records a 4x build-to-build swing in warm fit time across Julia 1.12 precompile images (13 vs 51 us on the migrad! path, since fixed), so microsecond Julia timings are fragile. The README says AI coding agents helped write the port and its documentation.

notes: Confirm at C. The README numbers match exactly (1.1x to 6.8x derived), and the metadata checks out: LGPL-2.1-or-later, 14 stars, 310 commits, last commit 2026-10-08 (active), registered in the Julia General registry. Correction: the C++ Minuit2 version is pinned (docs/UPSTREAM.md: GooFit/Minuit2 6.24.0, commit 57dc936), not unspecified. Shortcomings to record: the win is library overhead (Minuit2's per-FCN-call std::vector allocation and virtual FCN against a specialised Julia call site) on microsecond toy fits, not the language; C++ compiler unnamed; different random datasets on the gauss_ll rows; nfcn parity not shown; numbers from the May 2026 0.1.0-alpha gate against a 2021 upstream.

tier_reason: Independent third-party suite with public code for every side (nim/src/benchmarks/binarytrees.nim, cpp/src/binarytrees.cpp and .hpp, c/src/binarytrees.c; workload in run.js). C/C++ flags are in cpp/Makefile, and the Nim build commands, compiler versions and CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X) are in results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js. The record's runtime and memory numbers match the Binarytrees::Obj rows. Same tier and precedent as lang:java/kostya/langarena#binarytrees-obj.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: C/C++ 'prod' build: make -j prod with -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, -std=c++20 (clang 22.1.8, g++ 16.0.1 20260322 trunk), glibc malloc. The suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops, -flto=thin passed only at link), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, -flto=full at link) and PGO variants of every C and C++ test, all in the results file. Nim 2.2.12: Nim/Clang (the suite's 'prod' Nim row) is nim c --threads:on -d:release --cc:clang; Nim/GCC/ARC (a 'hack' row) is nim c --threads:on -d:release --cc:gcc --gc:arc. In Nim's config/nim.cfg, -d:release turns on opt:speed, so the generated C is compiled at clang -O3 or gcc -O3 -fno-ident -fno-math-errno, both with -fno-strict-aliasing. Nim/Clang uses the default ORC memory manager (Nim doc/mm.md). No build passes -d:useMalloc, so Nim's own allocator is used.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Nim/Clang (prod row, default ORC) 1.55 s and Nim/GCC/ARC 1.193 s vs C++/G++/Fast 2.098 s (the best of the C and C++ prod, Fast, Unsafe and PGO configurations; only the instrumented C++/Clang++/PGO/Gen build is lower, at 2.081 s), C++/G++ 2.101 s and C/Clang 2.482 s. That is about 1.35x faster at default and 1.76x with ARC than the best C/C++ configuration (derived from page data). The lead held in the three previous runs (2026-08-14 to 2026-09-18: Nim/Clang 1.51-1.55 s vs best C/C++ 2.02-2.15 s). Memory: Nim/Clang 102 MB and Nim/GCC/ARC 69 MB vs C++/G++ 70 MB.
corrections.why_faster: From the sources: the Nim test allocates each TreeNodeObj ref with Nim's built-in allocator (the build passes no -d:useMalloc). The tree is freed by the ARC/ORC destructor when 'tree' leaves scope at the end of run(), inside the timed region, just as the C++ unique_ptr destructors and the C free() walk are. The C and C++ tests call glibc malloc and free once per node (about 2.1 million nodes per iteration), and every C/C++ flag set lands at 2.08-2.55 s, so the gap is the allocator, not codegen. ORC rows (1.51-1.63 s) trail ARC rows (1.19-1.21 s), likely from cycle-collector bookkeeping, because TreeNodeObj is self-referential and not marked {.acyclic.} (inference). The suite's index-based Binarytrees::Arena variant reverses the result (C/Gcc/Fast 0.255 s vs Nim/Clang 1.049 s).
corrections.caveats: The win is allocation-strategy specific: an arena or pool allocator in C or C++ beats it, and the suite's Binarytrees::Arena rows go the other way (C/Gcc/Fast 0.255 s, C++/G++/Fast 0.53 s, Nim/Clang 1.049 s). The 1.76x figure is the non-default ARC 'hack' configuration; the default ORC 'prod' row gives 1.35x and uses 46% more memory than C++ (102 vs 70 MB). Nim's generated C is compiled at -O3, while the headline C/C++ prod rows are -O2; the -O3 Fast and Unsafe rows also lose. Nim's node carries a 64-bit int item, where C and C++ use a 32-bit int. ORC as the default and the -O3 mapping were checked in Nim's doc/mm.md and config/nim.cfg on the devel branch, not in the 2.2.12 tag. V (Clang) 0.806 s, Crystal 1.175 s and Java also beat C++ on this test; Rust (2.62 s), Zig (6.31 s) and C3 (3.4 s) are slower. LangArena calls itself a subjective benchmark, and its README says AI tools helped translate the tests. Each configuration is timed once per monthly run with no variance reported, though four monthly runs agree. Rows were selected by the search agent as tests where the language beats every C/C++ configuration; most other tests in the suite go the other way. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.

notes: Confirm at A. Runtimes and memory match the 2026-10-05 results file, and the lead is stable over four monthly runs. The Nim build commands and memory-manager details were checked in the results file, Nim's config/nim.cfg and doc/mm.md. Shortcomings to record: allocator win (Nim allocator plus ARC/ORC against per-node glibc malloc/free) that the arena variant reverses; the headline 1.76x is a non-default ARC build; single run per configuration; subjective, AI-assisted suite; prod C/C++ at -O2, though the -O3 rows also lose. Metadata checks out: nim-lang/Nim is MIT (some modules excepted per copying.txt), 18.3k stars, last commit 2026-10-11; LangArena is MIT with 41 stars.
